what_its_for: Streptomycin is an antibiotic used to treat serious bacterial infections. It is most commonly used to treat tuberculosis (TB), often along with other TB medicines. It can also treat other serious infections caused by certain bacteria, such as plague, tularemia (rabbit fever), brucellosis, and some types of endocarditis (heart valve infection).
how_to_take: Streptomycin is given as an injection (shot) into a muscle, usually by a doctor, nurse, or trained healthcare provider. You will NOT inject this medicine yourself at home in most cases. Each injection is usually given in the buttock or thigh muscle. Do not miss any scheduled appointments where this medicine will be given. If you are being treated for TB, it is very important to take ALL of your medicines exactly as prescribed, even if you feel better, to make sure the infection is fully cleared.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight, the type of infection being treated, and how well your kidneys are working. A common adult dose for TB is 15 mg per kilogram of body weight per day (up to 1 gram), given once daily or several times per week. For other infections, the dose and schedule may be different. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly. Never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a scheduled injection appointment, contact your doctor or clinic right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Do not try to 'double up' or take extra medicine to make up for a missed dose. Staying on schedule is very important, especially when treating TB. Missing doses can cause the bacteria to become resistant, making the infection much harder to treat.
storage: Streptomycin is stored and handled by your healthcare team or pharmacy. If you have been given vials to bring to appointments or for home use under medical supervision, store them in the refrigerator (36°F to 46°F or 2°C to 8°C). Keep it away from heat, light, and do NOT freeze it. Keep it out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine if it looks discolored or has particles floating in it — ask your pharmacist or nurse for a replacement.
what_to_avoid: Avoid other medicines that can harm your kidneys or hearing without first talking to your doctor. These include other antibiotics like gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin, vancomycin, or water pills (diuretics) like furosemide (Lasix). Avoid loud noises and protect your hearing, as streptomycin can affect your ears. Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you are taking. Avoid becoming dehydrated — drink plenty of fluids unless your doctor tells you otherwise.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: ringing, buzzing, or roaring sounds in your ears; hearing loss or difficulty hearing; dizziness, spinning sensation, or problems with balance; decreased urination or swelling in your legs, which may signal kidney problems; numbness or tingling in your face, hands, or feet; severe headache; skin rash, hives, or difficulty breathing (signs of allergic reaction); fever, chills, or worsening of your infection. These side effects can be serious and need immediate medical attention.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within a few days to a couple of weeks, depending on the type of infection being treated. For tuberculosis, improvement in symptoms like fever and cough may take several weeks, but it is very important to complete the entire course of treatment (which can last 6 months or longer) even if you feel well. Stopping too early can cause the infection to come back and be harder to treat. Your doctor will do tests to check that the infection is clearing up.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Streptomycin can harm an unborn baby's hearing and kidneys. Tell your doctor immediately if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. It should only be used during pregnancy if absolutely necessary and no safer option exists. Breastfeeding: Streptomycin can pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while on this medicine. Children: Streptomycin can be used in children but the dose is carefully adjusted by weight. It must be monitored closely because children's kidneys and hearing can be affected. Elderly: Older adults are at higher risk for hearing loss and kidney problems with this medicine. Doses are usually lower and kidney function is monitored closely. Kidney problems: If you have kidney disease, your dose will likely be lower or given less often. Your doctor will check your kidney function regularly during treatment.
